newsitem.title: USA: Arab groups pressure New Jersey governor on Israel.
newsitem.headline: Arab groups pressure New Jersey governor on Israel.

text.p: Gov. Christine Whitman, under pressure from Arab-Americans over her plans to visit a politically sensitive archaeological tunnel in Jerusalem and the Golan Heights, might not do so after all, a spokesman said on Thursday.

Whitman, a Republican of national stature who was at one time mentioned as a possible running mate for presidential candidate Bob Dole, was scheduled to leave the United States on Thursday on a week-long trade visit to Israel.

Arab-American leaders urged her to avoid going to the tunnel. Its opening in September by the right-wing Israeli government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu sparked a round of bloody clashes between Israelis and Palestinians that endangered the delicate Mideast peace process.
Whitman's official schedule also included a trip to the Golan Heights, territory captured by Israel from Syria in the 1967 Arab-Israeli war.
"We don't know if she's going to visit the tunnel," spokesman Carl Golden said. "It's up to her and her schedule when she is in Israel. She may or may not visit the tunnel."

Palestinians had said that the tunnel's opening was an attempt by Israel for greater control of the ancient Temple Mount area. Netanyahu charged Palestinian leaders with looking for an excuse to incite rioting.

At a news conference on Thursday in Princeton, New Jersey, representatives of the Arab American League of Voters, the Princeton Middle East Society and the American Moslem Alliance called on Whitman to stay clear of Mideast politics and keep her visit to strictly trade matters.

"A trip to the tunnel would further divide the Israelis and Arab community in Israel," said Morad Abou-Sabe, president of the Arab American League of Voters of New Jersey. "That is the direct opposite of what we want with the ongoing peace process. We need peace, not division."

He said he had received a letter from New Jersey's commissioner of commerce, Gualberto Medina, who wrote that it was "not her intention to demonstrate support or opposition to any foreign policy agenda" and that her proposed tunnel visit was prompted by her interest in the history of the site.
